passage: In the colony garden, Nandini announced, "I am the doctor!" and hung her grandmother's old dupatta around her neck like a stethoscope. Sunaina lay on the bench as the patient. Soon other children ran past with a ball, shouting. Sunaina sat up. "Let's play catch now." Nandini frowned. "No. I said I'm the doctor." "But it's boring now." Nandini's lip trembled, but she pressed the dupatta to Sunaina's knee. "Doctors don't stop in the middle." She kept checking the same knee, looking toward the ball game every few seconds.

qa.q: What did Nandini use as a stethoscope?
qa.a: Her grandmother's old dupatta.

qa.q: Why did Nandini keep playing doctor even while looking at the ball game?
qa.a: She felt torn: she had announced "I am the doctor" and going back on it felt wrong, even though she wanted to play catch too, which is why her lip trembled.

qa.q: What could Sunaina or an adult say to help Nandini switch games without feeling she broke her word?
qa.a: They could suggest the doctor finishes the check-up first and then goes to play, so Nandini keeps her word and still joins in.

qa.q: What is it like for Sunaina, lying on the bench while others play catch?
qa.a: Sunaina is bored and wants to join the ball game, and may feel stuck being the patient because Nandini won't change.

grounding: A young girl who announced she is the doctor refuses to change the game even when it stops being fun, because going back on her word feels wrong.

passage:
"I'm the doctor, Amma. You're sick."
"Okay, Doctor Minakshi. Oh, my tummy!"
Minakshi pressed a spoon to Bhavna's tummy.
Much later: "Minakshi, dinner is ready. Let's stop now."
"No! I'm the doctor."
"You look sleepy, kanna. Doctors can rest too."
"I said I'm the doctor. I have to." Her eyes were drooping.
"Shall the doctor go home? The patient is better."
"Is the patient all better?"
"All better."
Minakshi yawned and put the spoon down. "Okay. Doctor is going home."

qa.q: What did Minakshi press to Bhavna's tummy?
qa.a: A spoon.

qa.q: Why did sleepy Minakshi say "I have to"?
qa.a: She had said she was the doctor, and stopping felt like breaking her word, so she kept going even when tired.

qa.q: Which idea from Bhavna helped Minakshi stop, and why?
qa.a: Saying the patient was all better so the doctor could go home; it let Minakshi end the game while still keeping her word as the doctor. 😊

qa.q: What might Bhavna be thinking as dinner waits?
qa.a: She wants Minakshi to eat and rest, but seems to understand her daughter needs a way to finish the game that doesn't feel like quitting.

grounding: A small girl who declared she is the doctor won't stop the game even when tired, because going back on her word feels wrong.

passage:
Classroom note, Wednesday — Salma, nursery teacher
During pretend play, Elizabeth, 5, declared, "I am the doctor, and I'm the doctor all day." The others were happy for a while, then wanted to switch to a shop game. Elizabeth refused. She kept her toy stethoscope on and said, "I said it. I can't change." She sat alone in the clinic corner, watching the shop game, sad but firm. I sat beside her and asked if doctors sometimes buy medicine at shops. She thought about it, then walked over with the stethoscope still on and bought "medicine" from the shop. Note: she seems to feel bound by her own announcements. Offer ways to honour them.

qa.q: What game did the other children want to switch to?
qa.a: A shop game.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth saying "I said it. I can't change" show about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels her spoken word binds her, so changing the game feels wrong even though she is sad sitting alone.

qa.q: What did Salma do that helped Elizabeth join in?
qa.a: She asked if doctors sometimes buy medicine at shops, which let Elizabeth join the shop game while still being the doctor.

qa.q: How might the other children see Elizabeth's refusal?
qa.a: They may be puzzled or a bit annoyed that she won't switch, since they just want to play the new game together.

grounding: A nursery teacher notes a girl who refuses to leave her announced doctor role even when it stops being fun, because changing feels like breaking her word.

passage: Under the jackfruit tree in their village near Aizawl, Lalremsiami, five, put a string of beads round her neck. 'I am the doctor!' Shalini lay on a sack as the patient. Then a neighbour called that the new calf had been born. Shalini jumped up. 'Let's go see!' Lalremsiami held the beads. 'No. I said I'm the doctor.' 'But the calf!' 'Doctors don't leave.' Her lip wobbled as Shalini ran off. She sat alone under the tree, still holding the beads, looking toward the cowshed.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami put round her neck?
qa.a: She put a string of beads round her neck.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami stay under the tree even though she wanted to see the calf?
qa.a: She felt torn: she wanted to keep her word about being the doctor, but her wobbling lip and looks toward the cowshed show she was sad to miss the calf.

qa.q: What could an adult say to help Lalremsiami go and see the calf?
qa.a: An adult could say doctors visit new calves too, so she can keep being the doctor and still join Shalini.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel running off to the calf alone?
qa.a: Shalini is probably excited about the calf, and may not notice that a friend feels stuck and sad under the tree.

grounding: A five-year-old who announced she was the doctor refuses to leave the game even to see a new calf, because changing what she said feels wrong.

passage: Snow covered the preschool yard in Uppsala. Sofia, five, pointed at a sled. 'This is the hospital. I am the doctor.' Oskar lay in the sled and coughed loudly. Soon the other children began building a snowman by the fence. Oskar climbed out. 'Let's make the snowman now.' Sofia crossed her arms. 'I said I'm the doctor.' 'Doctor is boring now.' 'But I said it.' She stayed by the sled, stamping her boots, watching the snowman grow a carrot nose.

qa.q: What did Sofia say the sled was?
qa.a: She said, 'This is the hospital.'

qa.q: How can you tell Sofia wanted to join the snowman but felt stuck?
qa.a: She stayed by the sled stamping her boots and watching the snowman grow, while insisting 'But I said it.'

qa.q: What could a teacher do to help Sofia change the game without feeling wrong?
qa.a: The teacher could suggest the snowman needs a doctor check-up, so Sofia can join the others and still keep her word.

qa.q: How might Oskar feel when Sofia refuses to leave the sled?
qa.a: Oskar might feel puzzled and a bit impatient, since the game stopped being fun and Oskar wants to build the snowman.

grounding: A five-year-old sticks to being the doctor after the game stops being fun, because going back on what she said feels wrong.
